title: Delay-Suit Rails for Stuck Immigration Cases
one_liner: White-label filing infrastructure that lets solo immigration lawyers file mandamus/APA delay lawsuits in 48 hours, turning the government's habit of mooting suits into a flat-fee product.
customer: Solo and small immigration firms (1-10 attorneys) who pay a per-filing platform fee; end clients (naturalization, green card and employment petition applicants) pay the firm a flat $2.5-5k. Secondary buyer: employers with stuck petitions.
problem: Cases are stuck well past posted processing times: interviewed N-400s never scheduled for oath, I-485s and I-140s idling, and holds or pauses applied to nationals of dozens of countries since late 2025. Clients wait 12-30 months. Lawyers know a federal delay suit often shakes a case loose, but most solos have never filed one. Drafting the complaint, civil cover sheet, summons, service on the U.S. Attorney's civil process clerk, the Attorney General and the agency, and district-specific local rules is a 6-10 hour learning curve, and no one wants to be the first to file.
solution: A web tool with three parts. (1) An eligibility screen: enter the receipt date, form type and field office, and it compares them to posted times and to real observed outcomes, then scores the delay claim. (2) A complaint and exhibit generator with a per-district rules library, a service-of-process checklist and deadline calendar (the 60-day government answer window), and a template for the joint status report or stipulated dismissal that follows adjudication. (3) A docket-outcome database that logs, by district, judge and case type, how long from filing to adjudication. The attorney of record signs every filing. The platform is software, not a law firm.
why_now: Through late 2025 and 2026 USCIS added enhanced vetting, holds and pauses on benefit requests tied to nationality, expanded re-review of approved cases, and slower naturalization and green card scheduling. The volume of genuinely stuck cases is at a decade high. Federal courts are also less deferential to agencies since the Loper Bright decision, and adjudicating a stuck case is cheaper for the government than defending it. Solos are overloaded and short of billable-hour alternatives, so a ready-made product for a high-ticket service is easy to sell.
revenue_model: $350-600 per filing charged to the law firm (flat, not a percentage, to avoid fee-splitting rules), or $299/month for up to 3 filings. Later: a paid intelligence tier of docket-outcome analytics by district, and a litigation-funding partnership for clients who can't front the fee.
non_obvious_insight: The lawsuit is rarely litigated to judgment. The U.S. Attorney's Office usually tells USCIS to adjudicate within 30-90 days so the suit can be dismissed as moot, so the client's real purchase is a forced deadline. Clients almost never hear about this because form-prep firms earn on the application, not on pressure. Posted processing times are also misleading (they reflect only completed cases at a percentile), so whoever accumulates real time-to-decision data by field office and district owns the moat.
first_30_days: Recruit 5 immigration attorneys in high-volume districts (N.D. Cal., S.D. Tex., D.N.J., E.D.N.Y., S.D. Fla.) and offer free templates for the first filing. Build the intake screen and three complaint templates first (delayed N-400 after interview, delayed I-485, delayed I-130/I-140 or a nationality hold). Concierge-run 10 filings by hand, charging the firms $400 each. Log every outcome date, since that dataset is the product. Post outcome stats to immigration-lawyer Facebook groups and AILA chapter listservs to pull in the next 30 firms.

tournament.cluster: Immigrant households and workers: status deadlines and paperwork
judge_notes: contrarian: rank 2/25 - Suit is really a forced-deadline purchase; strong why-now; concierge-able in weeks; docket-outcome data is a real moat.
operator: rank 1/25 - Reachable buyer with instant ROI (lawyer bills $2.5-5k), urgent stuck-case demand, concierge start, and outcome-data moat.
vc: rank 5/25 - Real stuck-case surge, fast to sell to solos, outcome dataset is a moat; ceiling limited but concrete.

competitors.name: Bertollini / Mandamus.com (immigration mandamus boutique)
competitors.what_they_do: Law firm (NY, NJ, TX, MO bars; federal admissions in D. Conn., D.D.C., S.D. Tex.) that sells flat-fee mandamus/APA delay suits directly to end clients. Has a large SEO content library: pages per form type (I-485, N-400, I-140, I-765...), per district (D. Conn., D.D.C., D.N.J., E.D. Mich., E.D.N.Y., N.D. Tex., S.D.N.Y., S.D. Tex.), a case-law tracker, an EAJA-fees explainer, and a free Pro Se Mandamus Guide with complaint, summons and proof-of-service templates. Claims files most petitions within 10 days of retention. Publishes district-level voluntary-dismissal rates (EDNY, D. Conn., DNJ and EDMI at 83-85%, SDTX and DDC at 68-70%). No software, white-label service or co-counsel program for other lawyers found on the site.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Solo/boutique firm; bootstrapped. Claims 1,000+ immigration cases in 15 years and 30+ mandamus petitions personally litigated. Prices at $5,000 flat plus $500 court costs.

competitors.name: Docketwise (immigration case-management software)
competitors.what_they_do: The dominant practice-management and forms-automation tool for small immigration firms (forms, CRM, intake, billing, AI writing helpers). Its homepage and blog show no mandamus, federal-court filing or litigation features. It is the most likely incumbent to bolt on a delay-suit module, and the natural distribution channel or integration partner.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Not verified. Widely used by small immigration firms; funding and ownership not confirmed in this research.

competitors.name: Alma (tryalma.com, immigration law firm plus tech)
competitors.what_they_do: Tech-enabled immigration law firm focused on proactive visa strategy (O-1, EB-1 and similar) for companies and individuals. It says it is on an a16z list of top AI startups by spend. It shows no litigation or mandamus offering. It is a competitor for the law-firm side of the market, not the tool side.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Funding amount not disclosed on its site (a16z mention, Oct 2025). Claims 98%+ approval rates.

competitors.name: Boundless (consumer immigration services)
competitors.what_they_do: Consumer immigration case management with lawyer review. No mandamus or delay-lawsuit offering found on its site. It could add one as an upsell for stuck clients.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Venture-backed consumer platform (amount not verified here).

competitors.name: CourtListener / RECAP (Free Law Project) plus Lex Machina and Trellis (docket analytics)
competitors.what_they_do: CourtListener is free, open docket data on which the proposed docket-outcome database could be built. Lex Machina (LexisNexis) and Trellis sell judge- and district-level docket analytics. I could not confirm whether either covers immigration mandamus or APA delay suits with time-to-disposition metrics. The Lex Machina page fetch failed and Trellis returned 403.
competitors.scale_or_funding: CourtListener is a nonprofit with free API access. Lex Machina is owned by LexisNexis. Trellis is venture-backed.

competitors.name: DoNotPay
competitors.what_they_do: Consumer 'robot lawyer' for bureaucracy tasks. Its homepage shows no immigration delay-suit or mandamus product, so it is only a generic-AI-drafting substitute risk.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Venture-backed; also under FTC scrutiny for its legal-service claims.

competition.white_space:
Important caveat first. The WebSearch budget was already spent (200 of 200) before I started, so I ran no web searches at all. I used direct fetches of guessed or known URLs, CourtListener's API and GitHub search. This means 'no direct software competitor found' is weaker evidence than normal. One attempt to load a Google results page returned nothing and was not used. Before committing, someone should run 6-8 real searches (for example 'mandamus AI immigration', 'delay lawsuit software immigration attorneys', Crunchbase, YC, and the AILA and AIC toolkits).

What I found: no software or platform that sells attorney-signed, white-label mandamus filing plus a per-district rules library plus outcome analytics to solo immigration lawyers. The only direct-service players are boutique law firms selling the suit to end clients. Mandamus.com does this at $5,000 plus $500 and gives away templates, and the practice-management incumbent Docketwise has no such feature. The open data (CourtListener) and free guides make the raw ingredients cheap for anyone.

The genuinely unserved wedge is narrow. It is a pre-filing 'will this get mooted or dismissed here' triage, based on real district-by-form-type outcome data, plus a ready-to-file pack for routine delays in the districts where the government usually adjudicates rather than litigates (per Mandamus.com's own data: EDNY, D. Conn., DNJ and EDMI at 83-85% voluntary dismissal after agency action).

Parts of the pitch look weak against what I found:
(1) Nationality-hold suits look poor. Per Mandamus.com's summary of 13 D.D.C. delay decisions from June to August 2026, the government won all 13. Judge Leon in the consolidated Ivanov case found the categorical pause unexplained but dismissed the delay and mandamus counts under TRAC and limited relief to named plaintiffs. A 'nationality hold' template is a liability, not a hook.
(2) S.D. Tex., one of the five launch districts, is hostile. Cheejati v. Blinken (5th Cir. 2024) bars I-485 delay claims on jurisdictional grounds, and DOJ there files motions to dismiss rather than negotiate.
(3) Buckhannon: when USCIS simply adjudicates, the plaintiff is not a prevailing party and can't recover EAJA fees (typically $4,000-$12,000 only if a consent order is obtained). The flat fee holds up, but the 'forced deadline' product should be structured around consent orders.
(4) The '6-10 hour learning curve' is being eroded by free content and general AI drafting.
(5) The data moat is thin. CourtListener docket data is free, and the boutique firms already publish their own district stats.
competition.evidence_of_demand:
Moderate. The service is proven and paid for, but I found no direct evidence that solo attorneys pay for tooling.

- Paying customers for the lawsuit itself: Bertollini charges a $5,000 flat fee plus $500 court costs (https://www.mandamus.com). It also runs a dense funnel of pages per form type and district, which implies steady inbound demand: https://www.mandamus.com/uscis-mandamus-by-district.html
- Government behaviour that supports the core insight: 'USCIS often reaches out within 45 days to propose a consent order, or simply resumes processing within weeks of being served'; 45-90 day resolutions are common (https://www.mandamus.com). Voluntary dismissal after agency action runs at 83-85% in EDNY, D. Conn., DNJ and EDMI, and 68-70% in SDTX and D.D.C. (https://www.mandamus.com/uscis-mandamus-by-district.html). These come from one attorney's self-reported analysis, not an independent dataset.
- Structural demand drivers: the October 2025 end of the 540-day automatic EAD extension made I-765 mandamus a 'primary remedy' (https://www.mandamus.com/case-law-updates.html). Thirteen D.D.C. delay decisions in ten weeks show ongoing volume (https://www.mandamus.com/mandamus-decisions-summer-2026.html).
- DIY appetite: a free pro se guide with templates exists and describes 'high procedural risk' from service, venue and naming errors, which is the pain point the idea targets (https://www.mandamus.com/pro-se-mandamus-guide.html).
- Volume signal is mixed. CourtListener/RECAP is a crowdsourced subset, so treat these counts as directional only. Search 'Citizenship and Immigration Services' + mandamus + delay, by filing year: 2023 = 385, 2024 = 352, 2025 = 477, 2026 to date = 221. There is no visible 2026 surge in that sample, and the 'decade-high' claim in the pitch is unverified. Source: https://www.courtlistener.com/api/rest/v4/search/?q=%22Citizenship+and+Immigration+Services%22+mandamus+delay&type=r&filed_after=2025-01-01&filed_before=2025-12-31
- Not found: any RFP, forum thread or survey showing solo lawyers paying $350-600 per filing for a tool. Reddit was blocked from fetching, and no searches were possible.
competition.sharper_angle:
Drop 'delay-suit rails for everything' and become the outcome-intelligence and triage layer for routine delay suits, sold through the software solos already use.

1. Lead with the data, not the drafting. Build a district x form-type x judge database of filing-to-adjudication time, voluntary-dismissal rate, motion-to-dismiss grant rate, and consent-order versus quiet-adjudication outcomes. Source it from CourtListener/RECAP and PACER, and publish freely a 'will this get mooted in this district' score. Mandamus.com already publishes 7 districts of this by hand, so the defensible version is broader (all 94 districts), refreshed, judge-level and machine-readable, with the private layer being attorneys' own logged results.
2. Sell a narrow pack, not a general platform. Cover only routine delays where the moot-by-adjudication pattern is strongest: post-interview N-400, I-751, I-90, I-765 EAD renewals (the post-October-2025 primary remedy) and long-idle I-130/I-140, filed in the high-moot districts (EDNY, D. Conn., DNJ, EDMI and similar). Explicitly exclude or flag the weak cases, namely nationality-hold suits (D.D.C. dismisses on TRAC) and I-485 in the Fifth Circuit (Cheejati). Replace S.D. Tex. with a friendlier launch district.
3. Build in the fee logic. Include a consent-order-first settlement template and an EAJA/Buckhannon checklist, so the firm's flat fee stays profitable and any fee claim is preserved.
4. Distribute via the incumbent rather than against it. Ship as a Docketwise-integrated add-on, or a 'stuck case' triage widget inside case-management tools, since Docketwise has no litigation feature and already sits on the receipt dates and form types.
5. Treat boutique mandamus firms as customers and channel partners, not enemies. Sell them the analytics and overflow-filing capacity, and be careful with any referral economics because of fee-splitting rules.

Validate first with real searches (the ones this research could not run) and with 10 concierge filings that log outcomes. The go/no-go signal is whether 5 solos will pay $400 per filing when a free guide and a $5,000 boutique already exist."
